Research article · Project III · Central University of Technology

Electrical and Mechanical Effects of Adjustable Airflow on a 12 V DC Fan Motor Using an Arduino–ThingSpeak Monitoring System

K. Thabanyane and P. E. Hertzog

The short version

  • What I built: an Arduino and ESP-01 system that logs a 12 V DC fan’s voltage, current and speed to ThingSpeak while a 3D-printed vent restricts its airflow.
  • What I tested: three vent openings (100%, 50%, 0%) over 63 trials across seven days, with 1,668 voltage and current readings.
  • What I found: average current was about 18% higher with the vent closed, but the difference was not statistically significant (ANOVA, p = 0.26).
  • What I concluded: the system works for remote data acquisition, but without independent sensor validation it can’t yet serve as a dependable blockage indicator. The article sets out the improvements needed.

Abstract—Internet of Things (IoT) systems make remote fan monitoring accessible, but cloud logging alone does not establish measurement accuracy or distinguish restriction effects. This study investigates the electrical and recorded speed response of a nominal 12 V DC fan to 100%, 50% and 0% geometric vent openings. An Arduino Uno with current, voltage and Hall-effect sensors transmitted data through an ESP-01 to ThingSpeak. Three approximately ten-minute trials were recorded at each opening for seven days, producing 63 trials, 1,668 voltage and current readings and 1,665 speed readings. With the fan off, the firmware measured and subtracted the current-sensor offset at startup. After group-based outlier removal, mean voltage was 13.42–13.45 V and mean current was 0.358, 0.334 and 0.422 A at 100%, 50% and 0% open, respectively. The approximately 18% increase from fully open to closed was not statistically significant (ANOVA, p = 0.26). Recorded mean speed ranged from 4,833 to 4,947 RPM, but pulse-window timing and the absence of independent validation limit its interpretation. The system demonstrated remote data acquisition, while the experiment did not establish a dependable restriction indicator. Independent sensor checks, elapsed-time RPM calculation and direct airflow measurement are required to strengthen the conclusions.

Index Terms—Airflow restriction, Arduino, DC fan motor, ESP8266, Hall-effect sensor, Internet of Things (IoT), motor current, ThingSpeak.

I. Introduction

A useful monitoring system must connect sensor measurements to a physical question while accounting for measurement limitations. Cloud-centred IoT architecture combines sensing, communication and data services [1], providing a practical basis for remote monitoring of small electric machines.

Small DC fans move air in electronics enclosures, vehicles and ventilation systems, and the airflow a fan delivers depends on the resistance in front of it; when the path is blocked, the fan moves less air and its operating point shifts [2]–[4]. Microcontroller-based IoT systems have also become popular for monitoring motors, with Arduino boards, ESP8266 modules and ThingSpeak used to log motor current [5] and speed [6].

The cited blockage investigations focus on aerodynamic quantities [2]–[4], while the cited motor-monitoring studies demonstrate remote acquisition and speed monitoring [5], [6]. They do not directly validate this small-fan vent experiment. The practical question is whether the present low-cost combination can distinguish geometric opening levels after accounting for sensor limitations [7].

Closing this gap matters for inexpensive condition monitoring and for teaching: if the logged signals separate different restriction settings, they could later support detecting blocked inlets or filters, and if they do not, designers need to know the limits of such a system. This study only tests whether the signals distinguish the restriction settings; it does not test filter blockage itself.

This study developed an Arduino system with a current sensor, a voltage sensor, a Hall-effect speed sensor and an ESP-01 Wi-Fi module to log a 12 V DC fan to ThingSpeak, with a 3D-printed vent set to 100%, 50% and 0% open.

The research question is: How does increasing airflow restriction level to 100% open (low restriction), 50% open (medium restriction), and 0% open (high restriction) affect motor current, motor voltage and rotational speed of a 12V DC fan operating under constant supply conditions in the same environment, and what measurable trend between airflow restriction and motor performance is observed using ThingSpeak data? The experiment also evaluates which conclusions remain justified when airflow and independent RPM validation are unavailable.

Section II reviews the literature, Section III gives the project context, Section IV presents the methodology, Section V the results, Section VI the discussion and Section VII the conclusion.

II. Literature Review

A. Airflow Restriction and Motor Behaviour

Gifford et al. investigated two automotive fan types and found that downstream blockage reduced flow and altered the flow distribution; the relationship between blockage distance and performance depended on the fan [2]. Baniasadi et al. used CFD to examine upstream and downstream blockage of automotive axial fans [3]. Tang et al. combined experiments and simulation for an axial fan coupled to heat exchangers, identifying hysteresis near the stall boundary and possible blade-flow separation at high resistance [4]. These studies show why geometry and operating point matter, but their larger systems and aerodynamic measurements cannot predict the current response of this small fan. Direct airflow measurement would be needed to relate the present geometric settings to comparable aerodynamic quantities.

B. IoT Monitoring of Motors

Khan et al. presented wireless monitoring of three-phase motors using IoT [5]. Al-Shahethi et al. used optical speed sensing, Arduino processing, Raspberry Pi and ThingSpeak for DC conveyor-motor monitoring and control [6]. Their application differs from the present Hall-sensor fan experiment but supports the feasibility of sending motor measurements to a cloud platform. Gubbi et al. describe a cloud-centred IoT architecture [1], while Zachariah et al. examine ThingSpeak channel visualisations and platform design [8]. Together, these works support the sensing-to-cloud workflow and the use of comparison plots; they do not establish the accuracy of this project’s sensors or firmware.

C. Accuracy of Low-Cost Current Sensing

The ACS712 is a Hall-effect sensor with a nominal zero-current output of half its supply voltage. The firmware used 185 mV/A for the stated 5 A module. Rumpa et al. reported reduced disagreement with a reference instrument after regression correction [7]. A hypothetical uncorrected 0.1 V offset corresponds to approximately 0.54 A at 185 mV/A. However, a constant offset and offset drift have different effects on comparisons; accuracy depends on calibration, sensitivity, noise and stability. The present firmware measured and subtracted the zero-current offset at startup.

D. Comparison and Research Gap

The aerodynamic studies provide detailed physical measurements or simulations [2]–[4]; the motor-monitoring studies provide practical acquisition architectures [5], [6]; the current-sensor study highlights correction and reference comparison [7]; and the IoT sources explain cloud integration and visualisation [1], [8]. The present contribution is an exploratory comparison of three geometric vent settings across repeated small-fan trials. It combines voltage, current and recorded RPM with transparent reporting of the limits of those measurements, rather than claiming a universal or previously unstudied fan response.

III. Context

Institutional context. This project was developed as part of Project III in the Electrical Engineering programme at the Central University of Technology.

Project context. The project involved the design and implementation of an Arduino-based IoT system with a current sensor, a voltage sensor, a Hall-effect speed sensor and Wi-Fi integration, together with a Fusion 360 design for three 3D-printed vents that set a repeatable airflow restriction in front of a 12 V DC fan.

Educational context. The project aligns with graduate attributes such as problem solving, design, data analysis and communication.

IV. Methodology

A. Research Design

This research follows an experimental design with repeated trials, in which one variable is manipulated to observe its effect on others. The independent variable is the airflow restriction, set by a 3D-printed vent at 100% open (low restriction), 50% open (medium) and 0% open (high). The dependent variables are motor voltage, current and speed. Three trials are run at each aperture on each of seven test days. The fan, supply, blade geometry, sensor placement, sampling interval and room are kept constant, and no other fans are active.

B. Equipment and Components

The components are listed in Table I. The vent is designed in Fusion 360, printed in PLA and fixed 3 cm in front of the fan. It is about 40 × 40 mm, roughly the size of the fan, with a circular opening 38 mm in diameter (open area ≈ 1,134 mm²). At 100% open the circle is fully open, at 50% open half of the circle is closed so that a semicircle of radius 19 mm remains open (≈ 567 mm²), and at 0% open the circle is fully closed. Percentage open is the open area divided by the open area at 100% open. The vent is returned to fully open between trials. No airflow or pressure sensor is used, so the three settings are geometric restriction levels and the resulting reduction in airflow is not measured.

C. System Design

The ACS712 is connected in series with the motor (IP+ to the supply, IP− to the motor, OUT to A0), the voltage divider is connected across the motor terminals (midpoint to A1, lower leg to ground) and the Hall-effect sensor (5 V, ground, signal to D2) is mounted within 5 mm of a magnet on the fan shaft. All grounds are common. As shown in Fig. 1, data flows from the sensors to the Arduino and through the ESP-01 to ThingSpeak.

Fig. 1. Wiring and data flow of the measurement system. The schematic shows the planned Fields 1–4; the implemented firmware uploaded only Fields 1–3.

Firmware. The same firmware is used on all seven days. It averages 20 voltage samples and 50 current samples using an assumed 5 V ADC reference. Voltage is scaled by 5, and current is calculated from the offset-corrected sensor voltage using 0.185 V/A. Negative current results are converted to positive magnitudes. Falling-edge interrupts on D2 count Hall pulses, assuming one pulse per revolution. Whenever at least 1 s has elapsed, the firmware calculates RPM as pulse count × 60 and resets the count. It does not normalise by the actual elapsed counting time. Wi-Fi communication blocks execution while pulse counting continues, so the calculation immediately after an upload may be inflated; subsequent updates may overwrite it before the next upload. The effect on stored RPM cannot be established from the export alone. Fields 1–3 contain voltage, current and recorded RPM; aperture labels are stored in the spreadsheet. The configured upload interval is 20 s, and the observed median spacing is approximately 23 s. ESP send responses are checked, but the code does not verify a positive ThingSpeak entry identifier, buffer readings offline or retry automatically. Diagnostic text and AT commands also share the Serial interface.

Current calibration. The firmware used a sensitivity of 185 mV/A, consistent with the stated ACS712 5 A module; its “20A” comment was inconsistent with this numerical setting. At every system startup, the fan was switched off while 500 ADC readings averaged over approximately 1 s to determine the zero-current offset. This offset was subtracted in subsequent current calculations. The reported 2.5–2.6 V zero-current output therefore does not establish an uncorrected 0.54 A error. Residual offset drift, sensitivity error and ADC-reference uncertainty were not quantified. Taking the absolute value of negative readings can also bias measurements near zero upward.

D. Data Collection

Before each trial, the fan is manually operated for two minutes at the chosen opening to settle. The selected recording then lasts approximately ten minutes, with 25–29 observations per trial. The vent is returned to fully open between trials. Three trials at each of three openings over seven test days produce 63 trials. The exports contain 1,668 voltage and current values and 1,665 recorded RPM values. Readings are retained in logged order because some timestamps are irregular. The implemented protocol differs from the original proposal: the experiment uses an AC/DC adaptor rather than the proposed battery, approximately 23 s recorded spacing rather than 5 s, approximately ten-minute trials rather than twenty minutes, and seven days of repetition rather than nine runs overall. The reported analysis uses the implemented protocol.

E. Supply Voltage Verification and Sensor Calibration

The nominal 12 V AC/DC adaptor (model 1220; rated output 12 V, 2 A) was checked using a Fluke 177 multimeter. The recorded voltage averaged approximately 13.4 V, with raw trial means from 12.99 to 14.11 V. Of 1,668 readings, 32 exceeded 14 V and three were below 10 V. Thus, 97.9% fell within the stated 10–14 V comparison range, but the supply did not remain at exactly 12 V. The multimeter check did not provide a documented numerical uncertainty budget for the voltage channel. Current underwent zero-current offset correction at startup; independent current accuracy was not established using a reference ammeter. Running the fan without a vent established an unrestricted speed baseline, not a no-load condition or independent RPM calibration. No tachometer validation was performed.

F. Data Analysis

The export is organised by day, opening and trial. For the statistical comparison, each channel is screened independently within each day-and-opening group using the sample mean ± three sample standard deviations. Exclusions are applied once, and remaining observations are averaged separately for each trial, giving 21 trial means per opening. Equal weighting of trial means prevents longer trials dominating the group comparison. The 95% retention criterion is a completeness check, not proof of accuracy. Mean, median and sample standard deviation summarise the trial means. The arithmetic means are

x̄ = Σx / n (1)

where x is a value, n is the number of values and Σ means “add them all up”. The standard deviation shows how far values typically fall from the mean,

s = √[ Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1) ] (2)

The median is the middle-ordered value. One-way ANOVA and Kruskal–Wallis tests compare the 21-trial means per opening. Daily paired t-tests use the mean of the three cleaned trial means for each day and opening (seven pairs); they are exploratory, without multiplicity adjustment. The significance level is 0.05. The workbook graphs are reproduced from their original chart-linked cells: daily charts pool the available unfiltered readings, while trial profiles average Trials 1–3 at each reading index. They are therefore descriptive views of the workbook and are distinct from the cleaned, equally weighted statistical analysis. Later indices may contain fewer contributing trials. Reading index is not a uniformly spaced time axis. A current–speed correlation is not used to infer mechanical behaviour because speed is not independently validated.

G. Assumptions, Limitations and Ethics

The same fan, supply and sensor arrangement were used, while room temperature and airflow were not measured. A closed vent 3 cm from the fan was not assumed to form an airtight seal. Main limitations were the unmeasured airflow, unknown residual current uncertainty, absolute-value current processing, RPM counting intervals extended by blocking communication, lack of independent speed validation, short trials and timestamp irregularities. Trial means reduce within-trial dependence, but trials from the same day can remain correlated. Accordingly, unblocked ANOVA results are exploratory and daily paired comparisons provide a complementary analysis. Failure to find significance does not establish equivalence. The study involved no human or animal subjects or personal data and used low-voltage equipment under laboratory safety precautions.

V. Results

A. Data completeness

The dataset contains 1,668 voltage readings, 1,668 current readings and 1,665 RPM readings. Three expected speed values are missing. Channel-wise screening excludes 17 voltage, 7 current and 24 speed values, retaining 4,953 of 5,004 expected channel observations (99.0%). Retained counts are 1,651 voltage, 1,661 current and 1,641 RPM values. Some early recorded values are unusually low despite the manually applied settling period, including 0.24 V, 0.33 V and 120 RPM.

B. Cleaned trial means

Table II and Fig. 2 summarise the 21 cleaned trial means at each opening. Mean voltage ranges from 13.42 to 13.45 V. Mean current is 0.358 A at 100%, 0.334 A at 50% and 0.422 A at 0% open. The closed-to-fully-open difference is 0.064 A (17.9%); the half-open mean is 6.7% below the fully open mean. Between-trial current standard deviations are 0.204, 0.116 and 0.198 A, respectively. Recorded RPM means are 4,833, 4,947 and 4,898, a maximum spread of approximately 114 RPM or 2.4% relative to the fully open mean.

VI. Discussion

Voltage. The cleaned voltage means are similar across openings, consistent with use of the same supply, but this does not prove identical voltage in every trial. The fan is rated at 12 V, yet the recorded average is about 13.4 V. Some values exceed 14 V. The experiment therefore answers the research question under the recorded supply conditions, rather than under an exactly regulated 12 V condition.

Current. The mean of the 21-trial means was 0.064 A higher at 0% open than at 100% open, approximately 18%, while 50% open was lower than 100% open. The ANOVA (p = 0.26) and Kruskal–Wallis test (p = 0.06) did not establish a significant difference at the 0.05 level. The recorded direction was not monotonic across opening levels. Startup offset subtraction was implemented, so the measured zero-current output must not be treated as an entirely uncorrected error. Nevertheless, residual drift, sensitivity uncertainty and absolute-value processing were not independently quantified. The data suggests a possible difference but do not establish current as a dependable restriction indicator.

Speed. Recorded mean RPM differs by approximately 2.4%, with exploratory ANOVA p = 0.70. This does not establish that true fan speed is unchanged. The counting routine assumes one second despite communication delays that can extend a pulse window. Importantly, the upload uses the value calculated before the blocking send; a later inflated calculation may be overwritten before the next upload. The defect therefore creates a potential timing error, not evidence that every exported value is inflated. The export lacks pulse-window durations and an independent speed reference, so the size and frequency of any stored error cannot be reconstructed. The unrestricted baseline provides a comparison condition but not calibration.

Comparison with literature. The physical blockage effects reported in [2]–[4] concern airflow and pressure, which are not measured here. The changing current ordering therefore cannot confirm or contradict a specific aerodynamic mechanism. Remote acquisition is consistent with the monitoring architectures in [5], [6] and the cloud-centred model in [1]. The workbook overlays support comparison across conditions, complementing the emphasis on cloud visualisation in [8]. However, the separation visible on Day 4 does not establish a consistent seven-day electrical response. As in the sensor-correction work [7], reference measurements remain necessary to quantify accuracy beyond zero-current correction.

Anomalies and reliability. The low initial voltage averages in Figs. 4 and 5 and the low half-open RPM point in Fig. 8 are visible in the original workbook plots. Outlier screening reduces their contribution to statistical summaries but cannot establish their physical cause. The high retention rate measures available data, not sensor accuracy or successful delivery of every intended upload. Temperature, reference current, pulse-window durations and reference RPM were not recorded. Future work should separate serial diagnostic output from ESP communication, check the server entry response, implement retry or buffering, calculate speed from elapsed time, validate sensors, measure airflow and temperature, and randomise the order of vent conditions within day blocks.

VII. Conclusion

This paper investigated whether three geometric vent openings could be distinguished using voltage, current and recorded-speed data from a nominal 12 V DC fan monitored through Arduino, ESP-01 and ThingSpeak. Across 63 trials, cleaned mean voltage was similar at all openings and mean current was approximately 18% higher at 0% than at 100% open. The current difference was not statistically significant, and its ordering changed between days. Startup current-offset correction was implemented with the fan off. Recorded RPM did not establish accurate mechanical behaviour because actual pulse-window durations and independent speed validation were unavailable; the firmware timing defect is a potential error whose effect on exported values remains unquantified. The study demonstrates remote data acquisition and identifies measurement improvements but does not establish a dependable restriction indicator. Future work should use elapsed-time RPM calculation, independent current and speed validation, direct airflow measurement, and a randomised or blocked test protocol.
